analysis.one_liner: Makes it a crime to conceal serious product dangers from agencies, workers, and the public.
analysis.headline: The bill was introduced by Rep. Conyers with no cosponsors, sent to a House Judiciary subcommittee on January 22, 2015, and never advanced to a vote before the 114th Congress ended.
analysis.plain_summary: The bill would make it a federal crime, punishable by up to 5 years in prison, for a company or its managers to know of a serious danger in a product or business practice and fail to notify federal agencies and warn workers and at-risk people within 15 days. It would also make it a crime, punishable by up to a year in prison, to fire or punish employees for reporting such dangers. Any fines imposed on individual managers could not be paid by the company on their behalf.
analysis.who_benefits: Consumers who buy products, workers who handle dangerous products or practices, and any member of the public at risk from a hidden hazard. They would learn of serious dangers faster, because companies would face criminal charges for staying quiet, and whistleblowers would have federal protection against retaliation.

how_it_helps.text: Companies and their managers would face fines and up to 5 years in prison for knowingly failing to report a serious product danger to the appropriate federal agency and warn affected employees within 15 days of discovering it, or immediately if the risk is of serious injury or death.
Employers who fire, demote, or refuse to hire someone for reporting a serious product danger or warning other employees could face fines and up to a year in prison.

If an individual manager is fined, the fine could not be paid directly or indirectly out of company assets, so the penalty would fall on the person who concealed the danger rather than the corporation.
The bill explicitly does not preempt state law and preserves the right of consumers and employees to participate in agency and court proceedings, so existing legal avenues would remain open.

analysis.who_pays: Business entities and their officers, directors, and managers responsible for products or business practices, who would face criminal exposure for failing to disclose serious dangers on a 15-day clock, and who would bear the compliance cost of rapid reporting and employee warnings.

drawbacks.text: The 15-day reporting deadline and the broad definition of 'product supervisor' would expose individual managers to criminal liability for judgment calls about what counts as a 'serious danger', which could push companies into flooding agencies with marginal reports or into defensive practices that slow product development.

Businesses already face reporting duties under existing product-safety and regulatory law, so the bill adds a parallel criminal penalty on top of existing regimes, and critics would argue overlapping enforcement creates duplication without clearly improving safety.

The bill's instruction that it be 'construed in such a manner as best to represent and protect the interests of the public' gives courts broad discretion in applying ambiguous terms, creating legal uncertainty for firms.

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The public benefit is real: criminal penalties for concealing dangers, backed by anti-retaliation protection, directly target the cases where companies sit on known hazards. The cost side is the criminal exposure of individual managers on a tight deadline and possible over-reporting to agencies, but those are manageable design issues rather than reasons the public would be worse off with the bill than without it. On balance, the bill's benefits to consumers and workers outweigh its costs, and it died without debate or a vote.

outcome.mechanism: It was referred to the House Judiciary Committee and then to a subcommittee, where it sat until the Congress ended without a hearing, markup, or floor vote.

narrative.text: Rep. John Conyers Jr. introduced the Dangerous Products Warning Act in the House on January 6, 2015.
No other member signed on as a cosponsor during the entire Congress.
The bill was referred to the House Committee on the Judiciary on January 6, 2015, and to its Subcommittee on Crime, Terrorism, Homeland Security, and Investigations on January 22, 2015.
No further action was taken before the 114th Congress ended on January 3, 2017, so the bill never received a hearing, a committee vote, or a floor vote.

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: Manufacturers and sellers of products and services, and the officers and managers who would have faced personal criminal liability for failing to disclose serious dangers, are better off because the bill never became law. Consumers and workers lost the chance at faster warnings and anti-retaliation protection.

for.name: Rep. John Conyers Jr.
for.role: Sponsor; Ranking Member, House Judiciary Committee
for.what_they_did: Introduced the bill and gave introductory remarks on the House floor.

against.name: House Committee on the Judiciary
against.what_they_did: Received the bill on referral and never held a markup or advanced it to the floor.

against.name: Subcommittee on Crime, Terrorism, Homeland Security, and Investigations
against.what_they_did: Received the referral on January 22, 2015 and took no further action on the bill.

sides.party_line_note: No votes were ever taken and no member besides the Democratic sponsor signed on, so no partisan division appears in the record; the bill simply never moved.

industries.note: The bill would have imposed fines and up to 5 years in prison on companies and the managers who oversee product development, production, and quality control for failing to disclose serious dangers within 15 days. Its defeat leaves in place the status quo, where concealing a known hazard generally carries civil or regulatory consequences rather than criminal liability for the individuals involved.

The bill covered business practices and services in interstate commerce, not just physical products, so service companies with serious hazards would have faced the same disclosure and criminal-penalty regime. The bill's death means no such duty was created.
